summary_paragraph: A man with advanced HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, and a tracheostomy was admitted after accidentally dislodging his GJ tube at his nursing home. He was unable to take his morning medications and was found to have leukocytosis and tachycardia. He received IV fluids and a dose of metoprolol, which resolved his tachycardia. A temporary Foley catheter was placed to maintain the gastrostomy tract, and the GJ tube was successfully replaced the following day under fluoroscopic guidance. His leukocytosis improved without antibiotics, and urine culture showed mixed flora consistent with colonization rather than infection. He remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Chronic issues including HIV, seizures, COPD, and abdominal pain were managed with his home medications. The decision was made to remove his chronic indwelling Foley catheter as an outpatient due to infection risk. He was discharged back to extended care after a two-day stay.
